title: 451 | The Dystopian Novel Fahrenheit 451
subtitle: 451 degrees Fahrenheit is the threshold at which paper ignites, the work number of the protagonist Montag, and the title of this novel full of metaphors.
body:
## Those Who Save Fire

I remember a fairy tale by Zheng Yuanjie that I read before:

“The firefighters are going to save the fire.”

“Why save the fire?”

“Shouldn’t they put it out? It’s the house that needs saving.”

“All right then. The firefighters are going to save the house.”[1]

At the time, it only made me smile. But in this book, the world has grown so absurd that the firefighters’ profession has been completely overturned.

## Those Who Set Fires
From extinguishing fires to starting them, from protection to harm.

Fire carries different meanings in different stories. In the hands of Prometheus, who stole it, fire is hope and light. But in this book it is mockery and destruction.

Houses are already sturdy enough that a great fire cannot destroy them. What flames can devour is only books, and their owners. 451 degrees is the threshold of combustion, but is it not also the threshold of a civilization? When the world carried by civilization begins to go mad, destruction or rebirth hangs on the attitude toward books.

But note that the books described here are not actually paper books in the usual sense. When the world’s books have been burned down to a few scattered, unique copies, those possible last copies stand for civilization—for all the symbols, signs, and meanings created by those who came before. Once lost, certain meanings of that civilization’s existence can never be recovered.

> Spoilers begin here. You have been warned!!!

## Those Who Awaken
The male protagonist’s awakening occurs when he witnesses the firefighters ordering a woman to leave her house so they can burn the books inside. Calmly and silently, she refuses. She sets the house alight herself and turns to ashes with her books. Unlike the other firefighters’ accustomed numbness, his heart cannot settle. Fundamentally, he is full of love for this world, even when life is terrible, even when the society he lives in is deeply diseased, even when those around him have never noticed anything amiss. So when he sees someone willingly give up her own life, he begins to wonder: what is in these books that makes them worth dying for? What have they given her that allows her the courage to choose destruction alongside them?

I love the construction of this scene. I also believe that if such a diseased society really appeared one day, person after person would choose to burn with their books. They would follow one another, not be swallowed by the absurdity of the age, and become unnamed figures in its most absurd and tragic stories. Like the old captain standing at the Titanic’s bow and going down with his ship; like Socrates, who chose death even though admitting his supposed errors could have won him pardon; like Bruno, about to be burned in Rome’s Campo de’ Fiori yet still full of confidence in human civilization. I always remember Bruno’s proud cries in the fire:

“Darkness is about to pass, dawn is about to arrive, and truth will ultimately defeat evil!”

“Fire cannot conquer me. The world of the future will understand me and know my worth.”

The spirit of human civilization lies in this: matter will never stand above the mind, even when matter is the vessel of the mind, of the soul.

## Those Who Criticize
Another scene I love is the burning of the fire captain. Rather than saying he was burned to death, it would be better to say he actively chose death. The captain had read a great many books. According to the novel, his love of books in earlier years had bordered on obsession. But later, after various upheavals, that love turned to hatred. He hated books, hated their unreal worlds, hated the fractures their authors manufactured to pose as profound. I have not actually read many of the books he mentions; his denunciation of them all stirred my interest in reading them. But I think he also seems to represent another frightening extreme in our treatment of books. Unlike the majority of this age, who do not read, imagine an age in which everyone has read many books, but has only read many books—copying them into the brain as though copying to a USB drive. That would probably be another terrible age.

Books bring flowers, but also war; instruction, but also deception.

What matters is not the words in books, but all the things behind those words: breathing, beating hearts.

I tend to understand the captain’s suicide this way: when everything has lost its meaning, what difference can there be between living and dying? One remains alive only because an opportunity to die has not yet appeared. Montag, raising the igniter, gives him that opportunity. This feeling reminds me of a literary movement of the last century: absurdism, represented by *Waiting for Godot*. Godot does not exist. Waiting for something nonexistent is absurd, yet beneath that absurdity lies the anxiety and helplessness of an age. What is there to pursue? It seems there is nothing left worth pursuing. Likewise, when the difference between life and death is almost solely the presence of breath, and the pleasures of living seem less desirable than the peace of death, the captain’s complete lack of resistance in the face of death seems understandable too.

## Those Who Steal Fire

Finally, I want to discuss the book’s open ending.

From calling to save his wife at the beginning, to burning the captain in an act that appears passive but is actually active, to becoming one of the book-men, Montag’s development resembles a person’s awakening. He first saves his wife because he is tender and kind. Without that tenderness, there would be no conversation with the young girl about dandelions. Yet even someone so tender, when first encountering the world within books, can become arrogant and frenzied, wanting to overturn the world through violence. This resembles the mentality of many utopian writers throughout history.

But civilization’s development has never been advanced through bloodshed and oppression. Montag did not understand this then. He attributed everything wrong to society’s diseased system. As its direct embodiment, the fire captain seemed such that killing him would symbolize killing the diseased system itself. Later, however, Montag discovered he was wrong. Kill one captain, and a new one will appear. Such a diseased system exists because most people of the age tacitly accept its sickness. Violence cannot bring the spreading fire of civilization, because most people of this age have been soaked in salty seawater and cannot be ignited directly.

So the home he finally finds is among the Book-Men: becoming a certain book, and also a page of poetry within humanity’s spiritual civilization. A writer’s gentleness is sometimes not weakness, but persistence gathering strength for action. Passing things down from generation to generation, they wait for a new age. The threshold between that new age and the present dark one lies at Fahrenheit 451: whether most people of the age have reached a temperature at which books can ignite them, an attitude willing to give up the pursuit of sensory stimulation and seek fulfillment of the mind.

---

[1] The Chinese expression 救火 means “fight a fire,” but its individual characters literally read “save fire.” The dialogue plays on that literal reading. Quotations in this essay are translated as quoted by the author; they are not presented as verified historical transcripts.
